one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers the second part of his speech at the opening luncheon of the Asean Law Association's 12th general assembly -- companion to B06 (March 1). Asean is the 'darling of the world.' Some members like Singapore have attained First-World status; Malaysia and Thailand are exemplars on how to propel economies; and during the past few years, the 'VIPs of the world' -- Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines -- have exhibited enviable records of GDP growth. Why? Because the peoples' entrepreneurial spirit had been unleashed even if inadequately in some places; because permanent institutions are being strengthened and relied upon instead of upon the apron strings of temporary leaders; because educational standards have been uplifted and have released the spirit of the fisherman; because governments are learning that the best way of governing is to govern the least and to allow people to freely use their innovation and initiative, interfering only to check avarice and to level the playing field. Indeed, the primary role of government is to create just societies -- to focus on improving access to the basic necessities of food, clean water, education, infrastructure, healthcare, decent incomes and jobs; to honor commitments made in good faith; and to protect property rights. The peoples of the world and of Asean have different histories, traditions, cultures, ideologies, and mindsets -- but all of them need liberty and prosperity. Some countries, taking into account their unique backgrounds, start with improving their people's economic lives first and restrict temporarily in measured stages their political liberty; some others begin with political liberty thinking that their economy would flourish as a necessary consequence; still others rise with a combination of both liberty and prosperity at the very beginning. Such differing starts and focus are necessary in the growth of nations -- but eventually and inevitably, all the peoples of the world need and deserve liberty and prosperity in equal measure (the FLP signature passage). World Bank president Jim Yong Kim, an American of Korean descent whom CJ met during a reception hosted by PNoy, grimly said that 'the world's richest 85 people have as much combined wealth as the poorest 3.6 billion.' The 2014 ADB 'Key Indicators' show this glaring disparity is not as grotesque in the Asean region; indeed, Asean as a whole is fortunate to suffer less poverty and enjoy more affluence than many parts of the world -- still, CJ insists we cannot ignore the injustice of wealth inequality and the need to share prosperity. To illustrate: if our next-door neighbor contracts deadly dengue, would we not help him fumigate his house and drain the idle water in his yard -- because the culprit mosquito is capable of flying into our home, without respecting our fence and our legal certificate of home ownership? Of course we will, out of self-protection if not out of love. Similarly, if a bird flu epidemic breaks out in Cambodia, the neighboring countries -- if not the entire Asean community -- would surely come out and help eradicate the disease, remembering that the birds will not respect or care about the sovereignty and territorial limits of states. From simplicity really comes the wisdom of sharing and caring for the less fortunate, for the poor, for the least, lost, and last. The general assembly theme 'Sharing Prosperity at the Crossroads of Asean Integration -- the Legal Challenges' and the desire to solve the legal challenges that impede this altruistic goal should be foremost in mind when tackling, in full session or in separate workshops, the various topics drawn to meet these challenges. Some legal impediments to Asean integration of trade, investments, services, and skilled labor may be formidable -- like constitutional restrictions on ownership of land, media, public utilities, and natural resources -- and may take time to resolve. But some are really simple, like facilitating the opening of new businesses. Karl Kendrick Chua, senior country economist of the World Bank, in a speech on January 29, 2015, said that 'in the Philippines, it takes 34 days and 16 steps to start a business, and it costs 17 percent of per capita income, compared to 6 days, 3 steps, and 7 percent of per capita income in Malaysia.' Certainly, the lawyers of Asean can easily help solve this simple problem by tapping Malaysia as the model -- solving many legal impediments by simply sharing the solutions already formulated by Asean brothers. The simple problems can be resolved immediately during the assembly while the formidable ones can be planned more intensely in future meetings.
